response:
READING

**Setting the baseline**

The engines are the forcing event. The surveyor has said they will not see out the 2028 season, so a decision is not optional: Cormorant Sound Ferries must either re-power the Brindlemere or replace her, and it must do so before the end of the 2027 summer season at the latest.

Both courses are therefore on the clock, and both have been costed to a recognisable level of precision. What follows is an attempt to assess them fairly.

---

**The headline cost gap and what it actually represents**

TARNSIDE costs GBP 1,730,000.  
VELLACOTT costs GBP 2,680,000 net after the Kittiwake valuation.  
The gap is GBP 950,000.

On a single-year view, TARNSIDE is cheaper. But the fuel figure changes the picture. VELLACOTT saves GBP 190,000 a year on fuel. On that saving alone, the extra GBP 950,000 is recovered in exactly five years. After year five, VELLACOTT is running structurally cheaper every year for as long as the Suilvenaig operates.

Fuel prices are explicitly stated as "this year's prices," so there is uncertainty in both directions. But the Suilvenaig's advantage comes from her engine design, not from commodity pricing: the proportional fuel benefit would survive any plausible shift in oil costs.

The GBP 310,000 charter fee for TARNSIDE is a real, largely unavoidable cost. It covers twelve weeks in the winter (low-season) period, which softens the disruption but does not eliminate it: Sorrelbank Marine's vessel will have different handling characteristics, and it may not be identical in capacity to the Brindlemere. The risk of a charter falling through at short notice—illness of the relief vessel, a mechanical failure, a competing commercial commitment—is real and unhedged.

---

**The Brindlemere's age as a strategic problem**

The hull survey passed cleanly: no steelwork, no concerns raised. That is positive. But the survey was conducted when the Brindlemere was already thirty years old, and a re-engined Brindlemere will still be a 1995 hull when she re-enters service in spring 2027 at age thirty-two. Good for now, but the survey does not project forward fifteen years.

Spending GBP 1,420,000 on new engines is a large investment in an asset that, whatever the surveyors say today, is heading into the phase of her life where unplanned steelwork, electrical rewiring, and structural surprises become more common. The re-engining money is not lost—the vessel will work—but the effective useful life returned by that spend is harder to estimate with confidence than the balance sheet makes it look. A second major survey failure in five years would put Cormorant Sound in a much worse position, having already committed GBP 1,730,000 to a vessel that is no longer safe for service.

The Suilvenaig is a 2017 build. She is nine years old. A well-maintained passenger and vehicle ferry of that age typically has twenty or more years of working life ahead of her. VELLACOTT is not just buying a vessel; it is buying time—the kind of time that makes future planning possible rather than reactive.

---

**VELLACOTT's risks, taken seriously**

Three genuine concerns.

*Insurance.* The broker has not yet quoted on the Suilvenaig. This is the single most important unresolved fact in this decision. The Brindlemere's current terms are known and will continue under TARNSIDE. Any material increase in premium for the Suilvenaig erodes the fuel saving. If the annual premium were to rise by, say, GBP 80,000 the payback period on the cost gap lengthens to over eight years. I would not recommend committing to VELLACOTT until a quotation is in hand. However, there is no inherent reason why a 2017 vessel in good condition should attract worse terms than a 1995 vessel—quite the reverse, in most markets. The uncertainty is a reason to act immediately rather than a reason to reject the course.

*Manning.* Losing two of the nine masters is a material hit to the rota. Seven remains workable, but it is tight for eleven crossings a day through the summer season, and any further attrition becomes dangerous. The six-week endorsement course for the remaining seven needs to be phased carefully: the ferry cannot shut down while the entire roster trains, and the company should try to negotiate a staggered cohort. It would be prudent to approach the remaining seven privately and candidly now, before any commitment, to establish whether further retirements are likely. Two declared retirements are manageable. A third or fourth would change the calculus.

*Linkspan and transition sequencing.* The Suilvenaig is available from 2026-11-20. The Ardvraich linkspan modification costs GBP 240,000 but has no stated duration. If that work takes, say, ten weeks, the Suilvenaig cannot enter service until late January or early February 2027. Meanwhile the Kittiwake valuation on the Brindlemere expires 2027-02-11. The transition window is tight: the linkspan work should begin as soon as a decision is made and before the vessel arrives, the first endorsement courses should be under way by October, and the sale of the Brindlemere should be contracted before the valuation lapses. None of this is impossible—the November handover date actually gives twelve weeks of preparation from today—but it requires immediate and coordinated action, not a leisurely procurement process.

---

**What TARNSIDE does not fix**

TARNSIDE leaves the company operating the same route, on the same vessel, with the same fuel bill, on a hull that is ageing. The re-engined Brindlemere will be cheaper to run than a failed Brindlemere, but she will not be cheaper to run than a Suilvenaig. Five years after TARNSIDE completes, Cormorant Sound will have spent GBP 1,730,000 and will be operating a thirty-seven-year-old hull with cumulative fuel costs running GBP 950,000 above where they would have been under VELLACOTT—that is, the two courses will have broken even on cash, with TARNSIDE having delivered an ageing asset and VELLACOTT a vessel still in its prime. Beyond year five, VELLACOTT is ahead on every relevant metric.

TARNSIDE does deliver one thing VELLACOTT cannot immediately match: certainty. Known insurance, known masters, known infrastructure, known yard. For a seven-person shore operation, certainty has real value. But it is not worth GBP 190,000 a year in perpetuity if the operational risks of VELLACOTT are addressable, and they are.

---

**The balance of the argument**

VELLACOTT has more moving parts and more immediate risk. The insurance gap must be filled before commitment. The manning risk must be probed. The linkspan timeline must be pinned down. If any of those three investigations return a bad answer—if the insurance quote is dramatically higher, if further masters signal retirement, if the linkspan work turns out to take six months—VELLACOTT would need to be revisited.

But if those investigations are carried out promptly (they should all be possible within four to six weeks, which still leaves ample time before the November handover), and if the answers are within normal range, VELLACOTT is the stronger course. It delivers a younger hull, a better fuel position, and a more rational long-term asset, for a premium that is recovered within five years and continues to compound in the company's favour thereafter.

TARNSIDE is defensible precisely because it is lower-risk in execution. But it is also lower in ambition and worse in value, and it defers—does not resolve—the question of what replaces the Brindlemere when she reaches the point at which the hull itself becomes the problem.

---

CALL
  VELLACOTT

GROUNDS
  The GBP 950,000 premium over TARNSIDE is recovered through fuel savings alone within five years, after which VELLACOTT runs cheaper every year, while TARNSIDE commits the same capital to a 32-year-old hull that will continue to age and continues to carry a permanently higher fuel burden.
